statement: The historical and modern definitions differ In XVI, manuscript pp.~1--3, Loc~(1) requires isomorphisms, two out of three, and the implication \[ gf,fg\in\W\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f,g\in\W \] for $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. Loc~(1 bis) adds closure under retracts in the arrow category. Loc~(1 ter) says that $f\in\W$ whenever its image in $\Cat[\W^{-1}]$ is invertible. Loc~(2) concerns categories with a terminal object. The literal Loc~(3) is the absolute Theorem~A statement: $u:A\to B$ belongs to $\W$ if every $A/b$ is $\W$-aspherical. The relative Theorem~A in our conventions is printed as Loc~(3 bis), not Loc~(3) \citep[ms.~1--3]{AGGrothendieckXVI}.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 1–3; Loc (1), (1 bis), (1 ter), (2), (3), (3 bis), footnote 1
notes: Relative Theorem A is printed 3 bis. Modern strong saturation is not assumed for every historical weak localizer; the historical minimum is nevertheless W_infinity by A.19.

statement: The exact two excision axioms of XII Let $X$ be a small category, $U,V\subseteq X$ full sieves, $U\cup V=X$, and $S=U\cap V$. Every arrow of $X$ lies in $U$ or $V$, so the square \[ \begin{tikzcd} S\ar[r,"i_1"]\ar[d,"i_2"']&U\ar[d,"j_2"]\\ V\ar[r,"j_1"']&X \end{tikzcd} \tag{A.MV} \] is a pushout and a pullback in $\Cat$. XII, manuscript pp.~75--76, calls W(7 bis) the assertion \[ i_1\in\W\ \Longleftrightarrow\ j_1\in\W, \qquad i_2\in\W\ \Longleftrightarrow\ j_2\in\W. \] The second equivalence follows from the first by exchanging $U$ and $V$. W(7), manuscript pp.~76--77, concerns a strict natural transformation $f:X_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ between two such squares. With $0$ the intersection, $1,2$ the pieces, and $3$ the union, it says that any two of \[ f_0\in\W,\qquad (f_1,f_2\in\W),\qquad f_3\in\W \] imply the third. These are quantifications over all small categories and all such maps of covers, including empty intersections and empty pieces \citep[ms.~75--77]{AGGrothendieckXII}.
notes: Exact all-small-category and strict map-of-MV-covers quantifiers, with empty pieces and intersections included.

statement: Loc~(6), its three cube clauses, and Loc~(6$'$) XVI, manuscript pp.~16$'$--18$'$, uses the same map $f:X_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ of MV squares and defines \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm{Loc}(6a)&:& f_0,f_1,f_2\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_3\in\W,\\ \mathrm{Loc}(6b)&:& f_1,f_2,f_3\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_0\in\W,\\ \mathrm{Loc}(6c)&:& f_0,f_3\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_1,f_2\in\W. \end{array} \] After footnote~13, Loc~(6) means $(6a)+(6b)$, expressly excluding $(6c)$. On the single square (A.MV), Loc~$(6'a)$ is $i_1\in\W\Rightarrow j_1\in\W$, and Loc~$(6'b)$ is $j_1\in\W\Rightarrow i_1\in\W$. Thus XII W(7 bis) is XVI Loc~$(6')$, whereas XII W(7) includes all three clauses $(6a,b,c)$.
notes: XII W(7) includes all three cube clauses; XVI Loc (6) excludes 6c after footnote 13.

statement: Cofibrations and the four structural formulations For a functor $i:A\to B$, let \[ i_!:A\backslash\Cat\longrightarrow B\backslash\Cat, \qquad (A\to X)\longmapsto(B\to B\amalg_A X). \] The class $\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$ consists of the $i$ for which $i_!$ sends every morphism whose underlying functor is in $\W$ to another such morphism. XVI, manuscript pp.~25--27, states: \[ \begin{array}{p{20mm}p{112mm}} Loc~$(6A)$&Every $f:A\to B$ factors in $\Cat$ as $A\xrightarrow{i}M\xrightarrow{p}B$, with $i\in\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$ and $p\in\W$.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6A')$&Every Dwyer map belongs to $\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6B)$&Every MV square (A.MV) is $\W$-homotopy cocartesian.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6C)$&In every $\W$-homotopy cocartesian square (A.MV), now without any sieve or strict-pushout hypothesis, $j_1\in\W$ implies $i_1\in\W$. \end{array} \] Here $\W$-homotopy cocartesian means that the canonical comparison from a specified Grothendieck model of the homotopy pushout to the fourth vertex belongs to $\W$. Under enough cofibrations this agrees with the cofibration-replacement definition of XII, manuscript pp.~261--264.
notes: Intrinsic preservation definition; Dwyer means classical full sieve with right adjoint on generated cosieve; no false closure under retracts is used.

statement: Strict fibrations and the auxiliary classes For $p:E\to S$, the class $\Fib_{\W}$ is defined by strict base change: \[ p\in\Fib_{\W}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(u:X\to Y\text{ over }S,\ u\in\W\bigr) \Rightarrow\bigl(E\times_S X\to E\times_S Y\bigr)\in\W. \] We write $\W_S^u$ for morphisms over $S$ whose pullbacks along every $S'\to S$ lie in $\W$. A functor $E\to S$ itself lies in $\W^u$ when all its strict base changes lie in $\W$. The class $\mathcal F_{\W}$ consists of Grothendieck fibrations $p:E\to S$ whose reindexing functors $\alpha^*:E_t\to E_s$, for every $\alpha:s\to t$ in $S$, lie in $\W$. XVI, manuscript pp.~27--32, calls $p$ weakly $\W$-fibrant if, for every $T'\to T$ over $S$ with $T,T'$ contractible in the category-homotopy sense, $E\times_S T'\to E\times_S T$ is in $\W$. This defines $\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W}$. Finally, $\Parf_{\W}$ means both $\W$-smooth and $\W$-proper. The manuscript has \[ \Parf_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W},\quad \mathcal F_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W},\quad \Fib_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W}. \] These are different classes; a Grothendieck fibration is not, by definition, a member of $\Fib_{\W}$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 27–32; intrinsic, Grothendieck, weak and perfect fibrations
notes: Strict base change is distinguished from homotopy pullback and from Grothendieck fibration; variance of reindexing maps is explicit.

statement: The exact fibration axioms XVI, manuscript pp.~38--45, defines Loc~(7) to mean Loc~$(7a)$: \[ \mathrm{Loc}(7a):\quad \mathcal F_{\W}\subseteq\Fib_{\W}. \] Loc~$(7b)$ says that, whenever $p:X\to S$ and $q:Y\to S$ belong to $\mathcal F_{\W}$, a functor $f:X\to Y$ over $S$ with $f\in\W$ lies in $\W_S^u$. Equivalently in this situation, every strict fibre map $f_s:X_s\to Y_s$ lies in $\W$. Loc~$(7c)$ says \[ \mathcal F_{\W}\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \] For a reference localizer $V\subseteq\W$, Loc~$(7D_V)$ is \[ \Parf_V\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \] Loc~$(7D)$ without a subscript means $V=\W$. The weakest reference version singled out by the manuscript is $D_{W_\omega}$, with its historical minimum $W_\omega$; the modern version used in this paper is $D_{\Winfty}$. Loc~$(7F)$ means that every functor $f:X\to Y$ admits a factorization \[ X\xrightarrow{u}E\xrightarrow{p}Y, \qquad u\in\W,\quad p\in\Fib_{\W}. \] For fundamental localizers, all $X\to e$ belong to $\Fib_{\W}$, by product stability. Thus the associated category of fibrant objects has all objects fibrant. The word ``cofibrations'' in the initial formulation of $(7F)$ on manuscript p.~39 is a variance error; the subsequent formulations explicitly say fibrations.
notes: The word cofibrations in the first 7F wording is a variance error; reference D_V and absolute D_W are separated.

statement: The four other numbered conditions used in the audit Loc~(4), XVI manuscript p.~8, is \[ \coprod_{i\in I}u_i\in\W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_i\in\W\text{ for every }i\in I \] for every small family, including $I=\varnothing$. Loc~(5), manuscript p.~12, is $\W\subseteq\W_0$, where $\W_0$ consists of functors inducing bijections on connected components. Loc~(8), manuscript pp.~71--72, is closure of $\W$ under all small filtered colimits in the arrow category of $\Cat$; Loc~(8 bis) asks only for sequential colimits. Loc~(9), manuscript pp.~74--75, says that $\W$ is an accessible full subcategory of the arrow category, with its inclusion accessible. It does not mean preservation of every filtered colimit.
notes: All filtered colimits is stronger than accessibility. The source uses a countable-cardinality convention distinct from modern finite accessibility.

statement: Brown's lemma in the form needed in XVI 3.2.1 Let $\mathcal M$ have an initial object $0$ and let $C,\W\subseteq\Fl(\mathcal M)$. Assume that $\W$ contains identities and satisfies two out of three; $C$ contains isomorphisms and all $0\to X$, is closed under composition and pushout, and all pushouts along maps in $C$ exist; every map factors as a map in $C$ followed by a map in $\W$; and pushouts of maps in $C\cap\W$ belong to $C\cap\W$. Then $C\subseteq\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$. Neither strong saturation nor closure of $C$ under retracts is needed.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Lemma 3.2.1, ms. 20–22; XII footnote 136, ms. 266
notes: Complete typed relative Brown argument supplied; no retract closure of the cofibration class or strong saturation is needed.

statement: The consequences of enough cofibrations and their duals Let $\W$ contain identities and satisfy two out of three. Suppose pushouts exist and every morphism of $\mathcal M$ factors as a $\W$-cofibration followed by a $\W$-equivalence. Then \[ \operatorname{Cof}_{\W}\cap\W =\{i:\text{every pushout of }i\text{ belongs to }\W\}. \] Moreover, a $\W$-equivalence between objects cofibrant under a fixed $A$ stays in $\W$ after arbitrary cobase change $A\to A'$. Dually, enough $\W$-fibrations implies that a $\W$-equivalence between objects fibrant over $S$ lies in $\W_S^u$, and $\Fib_{\W}\cap\W=\W^u$.
notes: No implicit retract closure or abstract model-category lifting axiom. Exact assumptions are existence of pushouts, identities and two out of three, and intrinsic cofibration factorizations.

statement: The elementary implications between the excision clauses Using only two out of three and the definitions of MV squares, one has \[ (6a)\Rightarrow(6'a),\qquad (6b)\Rightarrow(6'b),\qquad (6c)\Rightarrow(6'a)+(6'b). \] Consequently XII W(7) implies W(7 bis), as Proposition~6 at manuscript p.~78 correctly states.
notes: Two specified degenerate cubes prove the arrows; repeated source label f_1=j_1 is corrected to f_2=j_1.

statement: The missing cofibration premise and its repair For the modern fundamental-localizer convention, Loc~$(6a)$, $(6'a)$, $(6A)$, $(6A')$, and $(6B)$ all hold. The equivalences asserted in XVI Proposition~3.6 and its footnote~19 are therefore valid in this convention. The proof gap identified in XII footnote~136 is real in the argument as originally written: termwise replacement by maps in $\W$ does not by itself show that ordinary pushout preserves them. The Dwyer pushout comparison and the gluing proof in Part~B provide that missing premise without reverse excision.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Proposition 3.6, ms. 25–26, footnote 19; XII ms. 266, footnote 136
notes: Automatic for modern fundamental localizers, without reverse excision. Actual endpoint-product cylinder is used, not pushout-product.

statement: The reversible equivalences and the role of retracts For a modern fundamental localizer the following are equivalent: \[ \mathrm{Loc}(6b),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6'b),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6C), \quad\mathrm{Loc}(6),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6'),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6c), \quad\mathrm{W}(7). \] In a historical or abstract formulation where retract closure is not yet available, the proof of $(6a,b)\Rightarrow(6c)$ requires that retracts of $\W$-aspherical objects be $\W$-aspherical. This is weaker than asking that every arrow retract of every member of $\W$ belong to $\W$, but the latter suffices.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.7, ms. 22, 26–27; XII ms. 265–272
notes: Pointed cofibers and their cone-vertex sections are retained. The wedge comparison uses e→Z_0. Object retract closure suffices for the third clause.

statement: The formal fibration implication scheme Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of arrows in a category with the relevant pullbacks. Define \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm A(\mathcal F)&:&\mathcal F\subseteq\Fib_{\W},\\ \mathrm B(\mathcal F)&:&\text{every }\W\text{-map over }S\text{ between }\mathcal F\text{-objects lies in }\W_S^u,\\ \mathrm C(\mathcal F)&:&\mathcal F\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \end{array} \] If every map factors as a $\W$-map followed by a map in $\mathcal F$, then $\mathrm A(\mathcal F)\Rightarrow\mathrm B(\mathcal F)$. If identities belong to $\mathcal F$, then $\mathrm B(\mathcal F)\Rightarrow\mathrm C(\mathcal F)$. If in addition $\mathcal F$ is closed under pullback and composition and contains all terminal maps, then \[ \mathrm A(\mathcal F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathrm B(\mathcal F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathrm C(\mathcal F). \] These are the precise premises of XVI Lemmas~4.4.1 and~4.4.3.
notes: Every Brown premise is stated; enough fibrations alone does not identify arbitrary weak or Grothendieck fibrations with intrinsic fibrations.

statement: Replacement transfers the weak-fibration formulations Suppose two classes $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ have the following comparison property: each $p:X\to S$ in $\mathcal F$ factors as \[ X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\overline p}S, \qquad j\in\W_S^u,\quad\overline p\in\mathcal G. \] Then $\mathrm A(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm A(\mathcal F)$ and $\mathrm C(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm C(\mathcal F)$. If the replacements are functorial over $S$ on morphisms between objects in $\mathcal F$, then also $\mathrm B(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm B(\mathcal F)$.
notes: The B transfer requires functorial replacements over the fixed base, not merely objectwise existence.

statement: The complete list of additional arrows asserted in XVI \S4 Besides the formal implications just proved, XVI, manuscript pp.~45--70, asserts the following. For $V\subseteq\W$ one has \[ \mathrm A_V\Rightarrow\mathrm B_V\Rightarrow\mathrm C_V\Rightarrow D_V\Rightarrow(7F), \] and the same chain with $V=\W$. It asserts \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm A_\W&\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\mathrm C_\W+\mathcal F_\W\text{ closed under composition}\bigr) \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\mathrm C_\W+\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_\W\text{ closed under composition}\bigr). \end{aligned} \] It asserts $\mathrm A_V\Leftrightarrow\mathrm B_V\Leftrightarrow\mathrm C_V$ if $\mathcal F_V$ is closed under composition, in particular if $V$ satisfies Loc~(7). Its summary 4.4.13 additionally asserts that sequential-colimit closure of $V$ makes all four reference conditions equivalent; sequential-colimit closure of both $V$ and $\W$ makes all eight conditions equivalent; and strong saturation plus Loc~(3 bis) for $\W$ gives $\mathrm B_\W\Rightarrow\mathrm A_\W$. The printed summary also says that $(7F)$ for $V$ suffices to identify the first three reference conditions; its earlier argument at 4.4.6 had used the stronger condition Loc~(7).
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 45–70; 4.4.6, 4.4.13, 4.4.15, literal heading 4.16 and footnote 36
notes: Records the manuscript arrows separately from their modern verification. The summary uses 7F for V where the earlier proof used 7; A.17 resolves the modern case.

statement: The weaker historical axiom system is not identified with the modern one here This audit does not prove that the literal historical Loc~$(1,2,3)$ with absolute Theorem~A implies relative Theorem~A, Loc~$(3\mathrm{bis})$. Consequently it does not use the modern strong-saturation theorem to settle the original eight-condition implication diagram for every class satisfying only that weaker definition. The unresolved statement here is precisely that implication between axiom systems; a first nonterminal test base is $[1]$, since the relative axiom over $e$ is tautological. The minimum $W_\omega=\Winfty$ is already settled by the distinct weak-localizer theorem in \claimref{A.19}; it is not part of this residual obligation.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Loc (3) versus Loc (3 bis); historical eight-condition implication diagram
notes: Open in this audit: absolute historical Theorem A ⇒ relative Theorem A. Test base [1] is the first nonterminal instance. Not a claim of newly open literature status; minimum itself is settled.

statement: All eight fibration variants collapse in the modern convention Let $V\subseteq\W$ be modern fundamental localizers. Each of the eight conditions $\mathrm A_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm B_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm C_\W,\allowbreak D_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm A_V,\allowbreak\mathrm B_V,\allowbreak\mathrm C_V,\allowbreak D_V$ is equivalent to \[ \W=\Winfty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\W=\Fl(\Cat). \] No accessibility or filtered-colimit hypothesis is needed for this conclusion. Thus every conditional arrow in \claimref{A.15} is valid for the modern convention, including the summary's $(7F)$-for-$V$ formulation, although that formulation is not what the earlier manuscript proof establishes.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 45–70 and 83–85; all eight fibration formulations
notes: No accessibility hypothesis. All eight conditions imply homotopy-pullback stability, then W=W_infinity or total; cited full proof E.4–E.5.

statement: The coproduct consequences accompanying the implication diagram Write Loc~$(4a_0)$ for preservation of finite coproducts of equivalences, Loc~$(4a)$ for preservation of all small coproducts, and Loc~$(4b)$ for reflection of equivalences by coproducts of families with a common indexing set. The assertions surrounding XVI \S3 and used in \S4 are \[ (6a)\Rightarrow(4a_0),\qquad (6a)+(8)\Rightarrow(4a),\qquad (7)\Rightarrow(4b). \] Consequently $(6a)+(7)+(8)$ implies Loc~$(4)$. In the modern convention $(4a)$ already follows from relative Theorem~A; no reverse excision is needed for any of these assertions.
notes: Includes arbitrary small indexing sets and empty summands; modern forward coproduct closure needs no extra Loc (8).

statement: The literal historical minimum is also the weak-homotopy localizer Let $W_\omega$ denote the intersection of all classes satisfying the literal XVI Loc~$(1,2,3)$, where Loc~$(3)$ is absolute Theorem~A. Then \[ W_\omega=\Winfty. \] This equality does not require identifying every weak fundamental localizer with a modern fundamental localizer.
notes: Known separate weak-localizer theorem. Literal Loc1 cancellation implies Cisinski FS3, so the minimality theorem applies without relative Theorem A.

statement: The distinction needed to classify the manuscript's uses In the modern convention, forward homotopy-pushout invariance is available for every fundamental localizer. A statement asserting reverse cancellation for \emph{all} homotopy-pushout squares is equivalent to the conditions of \claimref{B.5}. The weaker assertion that the intersection and union of two sieves are aspherical only requires forward gluing and retract closure to imply that the pieces are aspherical. It does not imply reverse cancellation for maps of such squares.
notes: Object-level intersection/union implication is true for every modern W by forward gluing and retracts; it must not be equated with the failed map-level 6c.

statement: The global reverse claims at the start of XII \S5 XII Th\'eor\`eme~2, manuscript p.~78, and its interpretation of reverse excision as a property of ordinary $\mathrm{HOT}$ at pp.~79--80 are false. The forward clauses of W(7) and W(7 bis) hold for $\Winfty$; the reverse clauses, and the cube clause later called Loc~$(6c)$, fail. The conditional implications between those axioms at pp.~76--78 remain valid, with retract closure for the object-to-cube reduction.
notes: Finite A with 35 objects and 159 arrows, and its two cones; acyclic-group alternative also specified.

statement: Reverse cancellation remains false along genuine Dwyer maps The reverse directions asserted conditionally in XII Proposition~6, manuscript pp.~81--83, Th\'eor\`eme~3, pp.~108--109, and footnote~124, pp.~227--228, do not hold for $\Winfty$, even when the attaching sieve is a genuine Dwyer inclusion and all the source's boundary and closure conditions hold. Their forward directions are valid. The full conditional statements are valid when the appropriate reverse axiom is assumed.
notes: Reverse cancellation fails even for a genuine Dwyer cofibration; full reverse hypotheses repair the conditional claims.

statement: The one-point-complement converse The one-point-complement equivalence at XII, manuscript p.~85, and again Corollaries~4--5, pp.~149--151, is valid under W(7 bis), but false for $\Winfty$. So are reverse formulations in Proposition~7, pp.~84--85, when specialized to a one-point complement. Their direct implication from aspherical comma categories is valid for every fundamental localizer.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 85, 149–151; Proposition 7 and one-point-complement tests
notes: One-point complement is required to have only the identity endomorphism; the reverse assertion is conditional on full excision.

statement: The total-asphericity gluing argument has a separate error XII Proposition~9(b), manuscript pp.~97--98, its retraction-based repair at pp.~98--100, and its conclusion that the outgoing fork is totally aspherical are false even for $\W=\W_R$ with $R$ any nonzero commutative ring. These errors persist when full W(7) is valid. The additional retractions do not make the relevant left Kan extension preserve monomorphisms or intersections.
notes: Four objects and ten arrows give S^2; an ordinary final fork is contractible. The mono-under-right-adjoint claim about Kan extension is independently false.

statement: The suspension construction used to disprove cofibrancy survives The counterexample mechanism of XII, manuscript pp.~104--107, survives for $\Winfty$ when its auxiliary category $Y$ is nonempty and simply connected. Its conclusion that the resulting $X'$ is weakly contractible exactly when $Y$ is weakly contractible has an independent proof. The analogous appendix calculation at manuscript pp.~15--16 has the advertised noncofibrancy conclusion, but its displayed fundamental-group calculation is false.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 104–107; appendix ms. 15–16; XIIba-C008,C012,C016; XIIapp-C060–065
notes: Appendix V′_0 is S^2, not S^1; its double cone is S^3. The later equivalence transfer uses forward trivial-Dwyer pushout, not reverse cancellation. Explicit finite original attachment checked.

statement: What the integral-square arguments actually require XII Proposition~13, manuscript pp.~125--126, its cube corollary at pp.~127--128, the homotopy-cocartesian formulations at pp.~132--135, and their proper-integral duals are valid with their stated full reverse assumptions. Their forward clauses, the construction of the integral models, and the comparison with the closed-cover model require no reverse axiom. Their reverse clauses are false for $\Winfty$.
notes: Forward and reverse clauses separated; no inference merely from an abstract isomorphism in the localized category.

statement: The reverse smoothness theorem has an explicit finite counterexample The reverse direction of XII Th\'eor\`eme~4(a), manuscript pp.~146--147, and its local version in Corollary~6(b), p.~157, are false for $\Winfty$ when the strong W(7 bis) hypothesis is removed. The forward theorem and Corollaries~1--3, pp.~147--149, are valid without reverse excision. The reverse assertions remain valid under their stated full W(7 bis) hypothesis.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII Theorem 4, ms. 146–149; Corollary 6, ms. 157; XIIb-b-B035–038,B042–046; XIIbb-C011–020
notes: 110 objects and 1051 arrows; exceptional central lift has 107 objects and 867 arrows. All lifting categories and finite compositions checked. The conditional reverse theorem is retained.

statement: The presheaf theorem's converses fail, while its pushout assertion survives For a small category $X$, a pushout square of presheaves on $X$ with one leg a monomorphism gives the homotopy-pushout comparison asserted in XII Th\'eor\`eme~5, manuscript p.~168, for every modern fundamental localizer. The two forward equivalence implications hold. The two converses stated there under strong W(7 bis) are false for $\Winfty$ without that hypothesis.
notes: Exact nerve formula N(X/F)_n=disjoint_union_chains F(x_n) proves colimit/mono preservation. Counterexample uses all simplex categories of finite nerves and includes degenerate simplices.

statement: Cofibrancy does not recognize the manuscript's boundary condition The assertion at XII, manuscript p.~111, that a $\W$-cofibration sieve with one-point complement is necessarily $\W$-dwyerienne is false. So is its asserted consequence that cofibrancy after every change of the complementary category forces that boundary condition. These failures occur for $\Winfty$, for all $\W_n$, and for $\W_R$ with $R\ne0$, including localizers satisfying full W(7).
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 111; companion XIIba-C037–038; TOTASPH boundary-weight recognition claim
notes: Two parallel arrows; universal cofibrancy proof covers every complementary base change, including the empty complement. The narrower question about trivial cofibrations is not refuted by this example.

statement: The actual cylinder and cofibration formalism survive The factorizations and enough-cofibration results at XII, manuscript pp.~228--234, and Proposition~16 at pp.~231--232 are valid for every modern fundamental localizer. They use the product of the endpoint inclusion with the source category. They do not require the pushout-product stability sought at pp.~114--115. The reverse clauses in footnote~124 are the false extra assertions isolated in \claimref{G.3}.
notes: The actual cylinder is a product followed by pushout, n≥2. H.6 refutes the distinct endpoint pushout-product desideratum.

statement: Pasting homotopy-pushout squares does not use reverse excision XII Proposition~17, manuscript pp.~234--235, and Proposition~18, pp.~236--239, hold for every modern fundamental localizer. In particular, if the left square in a rectangle is $\W$-homotopy cocartesian, the right square is $\W$-homotopy cocartesian if and only if the outer rectangle is. This is cancellation of \emph{pushout squares}, not reflection of equivalences along pushout.
notes: Pasting cancellation concerns squares, not reflection of equivalences along a pushout. Only forward direction of the source biconditional is used.

statement: The intervening fibre theory has no reverse-cofibration dependency The theory of $\W$-fibrations and homotopy-cartesian squares in XII, manuscript pp.~240--261, uses the factorization axiom ``enough $\W$-fibrations'' and its stated terminal-object hypothesis, not W(7 bis) in reverse. In $\Cat$, the all-objects-fibrant hypothesis is automatic from product stability. These results therefore apply whenever Loc~$(7F)$ holds, even when Loc~$(6b)$ fails.
notes: Loc (7F) and all-terminal-fibrant assumptions are explicit. In Cat the latter follows from product stability.

statement: The two definitions of homotopy-cocartesian square agree XII Proposition~20, manuscript pp.~262--264, is valid for every modern fundamental localizer: the Grothendieck-integral criterion for a homotopy-cocartesian square agrees with the criterion using a $\W$-cofibration replacement and ordinary pushout. Its invocation of the strong relative Theorem~A axiom is legitimate under our conventions, and no reverse excision is required.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII Proposition 20, ms. 262–264; footnote 134; XVI footnotes 15–17, ms. 23–24
notes: Direction of the comparison lambda in the source is reversed; correcting the arrow preserves the proof by two out of three.

statement: The opening assertion and the gap of XII \S8 need different repairs The opening sentence of XII \S8, manuscript p.~265, reverses the implication proved in Proposition~6 at p.~78. The actual earlier result is W(7)$\Rightarrow$W(7 bis). The proposition stated immediately thereafter, deriving the forward and reverse cube clauses from W(7 bis) and the third clause with retract closure, is valid in the modern convention. Footnote~136 at p.~266 identifies a real missing comparison in its proof, which is supplied by \claimref{A.8}--\claimref{A.12}.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 265–267; reversed citation of Proposition 6 and footnote 136
notes: The citation at p.265 reverses the result at p.78. Footnote136 identifies a real missing pushout comparison, now supplied without circularity.

statement: The cofibres lemma survives, but the reduction uses reverse detection The lemma at XII, manuscript p.~268, is true for every modern fundamental localizer: for a map of homotopy-pushout squares, the square of its four pointed homotopy cofibres is again a homotopy-pushout square. The assertion at pp.~269--270 that the \emph{whole reduction} of W(7) to aspherical vertices has used only the forward clause is false. The proof has already used cofibres to reflect equivalences at p.~267.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII lemma and deployment argument, ms. 268–272
notes: Fubini for pointed homotopy cofibers proves the lemma; the map-to-object reduction already used reverse cofiber detection at p.267.

statement: The abstract cube clause and its first corollary are false as printed Theorem~3\,$^\circ$ at XII, manuscript p.~274, claims $f_0,f_3\in\W\Rightarrow f_1,f_2\in\W$ from enough cofibrations, a terminal object, and closure of aspherical objects under retracts. It is false. Corollary~1 on the same page, identifying this map assertion with its aspherical-object version, is also false without the missing reverse-detection hypothesis. Both failures already occur in $(\Cat,\Winfty)$.

notes: A strict finite cube satisfies every printed hypothesis and fails 6c. The PDF confirms absence of conservativity in theorem3°; adding it repairs the assertion.

statement: The literal Cartesian version of Cons~2 is false At XII, manuscript p.~273, the condition named Cons~2 says ``carr\'e cart\'esien''. Read literally, its claim is false even for $\W_Z$. It therefore is not equivalent to the conservativity axiom stated immediately above it. Replacing ``cart\'esien'' by ``cocart\'esien'', retaining the two cofibration hypotheses, gives the valid intended implication.

notes: Empty strict pullback of the distinct endpoints of [1], with all three other vertices contractible; false even for W_Z. Changing Cartesian to cocartesian gives the intended statement.

statement: A sieve and its complementary cosieve always give the proposed homotopy pushout Let $U$ be a full sieve in a small category $X$, and let $V=X\setminus U$ be the full complementary cosieve. Let $E$ be the full subcategory of the arrow category $\mathrm{Fl}(X)$ on arrows $a:u\to v$ with $u\in U,v\in V$, with source and target functors $s:E\to U$ and $t:E\to V$. The source-to-target natural transformation gives a specified comparison \[ \hocolim(BU\xleftarrow{Bs}BE\xrightarrow{Bt}BV)\longrightarrow BX, \] and it is a weak homotopy equivalence. This proves the conjecture at XII appendix, manuscript pp.~17--18, for every modern fundamental localizer, without reverse excision. The extra reverse tests proposed in the same paragraph are false for $\Winfty$.

notes: Full category-level Quillen A proof, explicit P/x contraction and typed natural transformations; includes empty sieve, complement or crossing-arrow category.

statement: The final conditional theorem is correct after the stated repairs XII Theorem~1\,$^\circ$ at pp.~272--273, its equivalence of reverse cube cancellation with conservativity in part~2\,$^\circ$, and Corollary~2 at p.~275 are valid in $\Cat$ for modern fundamental localizers. Corollary~2 must retain its explicit conservativity hypothesis. The same corrected clauses hold in an arbitrary relative category under the precise pushout and factorization premises of \claimref{G.26}, which supplies the compatible finite homotopy-cofibre comparisons from those premises.

notes: Corrected theorem proved in modern Cat and extended to the exact arbitrary-relative-category factorization premises in G.26. The unconditional3° and literal Cartesian Cons2 remain false and are not used.

statement: The valid and invalid dependencies in XVI \S\S3--4 The implications in XVI Proposition~3.3, manuscript p.~22, summary~3.5, p.~25, and Corollary~3.7, pp.~26--27, are valid for modern fundamental localizers, with the qualifications on retracts specified in Part~A. They are conditional statements about reversible excision; they do not assert that $\Winfty$ has it. The cofibre calculus in Comment~3.4 and Proposition~3.6, pp.~22--26, and the digression~4.4.15, pp.~66--68, need only forward gluing. The arguments concerning fibration axioms throughout \S4 have no reverse-cofibration premise.
notes: Inventory includes the Brown premise, presheaf monos, integral models, the enough-cofibrations digression, and every fibration-arrow family.

statement: Theorem 5.4's list is false, but its accessibility assertion is true XVI Th\'eor\`eme~5.4, manuscript p.~79, is false when its list of axioms includes full Loc~$(6)=(6a)+(6b)$. Its assertions about accessibility of $\Winfty$ and its satisfaction of the other listed axioms remain true. The accessibility proof at pp.~80--83 does not need reverse cofibration excision.
notes: The full printed list is false only through reverse excision; direct countable witness construction and the combinatorial-model theorem establish accessibility without it.

statement: The reverse axiom changes the minimum in XVI \S6 The fibration theorem XVI~6.1, manuscript pp.~83--85, and Corollary~6.3 have no reverse-cofibration dependency and remain valid; in the modern convention their nontrivial conclusion is $\W=\Winfty$. In contrast, the full stability list proposed in 6.4(b), pp.~87--89, has total localizer as its least solution if it includes $(6b)$. There is no solution satisfying that list and the additionally asserted containment $\widetilde{\W}_\infty\subseteq\Winfty$. If $(6)$ is replaced throughout that list by $(6a)$, the least solution is $\Winfty$.
notes: Full stability minimum is total; if containment in W_infinity is imposed there is no solution. The forward-only minimum is W_infinity.

statement: Accessible localizers give derivators without reverse excision For every accessible modern fundamental localizer $\W$, the diagram-localization construction underlying $\mathrm{HOT}_{\W}$ is a strong derivator on all small indexing categories. No assumption of Loc~$(6b)$, Loc~$(7)$, Loc~$(7D)$, or Loc~$(7F)$ is required. In particular the remark at XVI, manuscript pp.~119--120, that $(6b)$ plays no role in obtaining the derivator axioms is correct. This statement uses relative Theorem~A and does not identify it with the weaker historical definition.
notes: Accessible modern scope; Cisinski Theorem5.2.15 and Groth Proposition1.36. Explicit projective/injective model presentation and both pointwise comma formulas; no 6b,7,7D,7F assumption.

statement: Locations and interpretation of the reverse dependencies The following register records the direct and inherited reverse-excision uses in the requested sections. A conditional assertion is recorded as valid only with its actual reverse premise; a redundant use in a proof is distinguished from a false conclusion. ``Forward'' in this table means the precise comparison and premise verified in the cited claim, not unrestricted preservation by ordinary pushout. The supplied XIIc-b excerpt continues through manuscript p.~275, so the register includes the three pages beyond the endpoint mentioned in the prompt.

statement: The factorization-only hypotheses supply the required abstract finite calculus Let $\mathcal M$ be a category, in a fixed universe large enough for the diagrams under consideration, with all pushouts. Let $\W\subseteq\Fl(\mathcal M)$ contain the isomorphisms and satisfy two out of three. Assume that every arrow factors as an intrinsic $\W$-cofibration followed by a member of $\W$. These are the pushout-dual premises of XII \S7 and the factorization premise at manuscript p.~272. They suffice for a choice-independent notion of homotopy-pushout square, with specified weak comparison maps between its models, invariance under objectwise $\W$-maps, and the compatible finite comparisons needed for the square-of-cofibres lemma at p.~268. If $\mathcal M$ has a terminal object $e$, that lemma holds for the actual cofibres of a map of homotopy-pushout squares whose four vertical maps are cofibrations. Under these same hypotheses, theorem parts~1\,$^\circ$--2\,$^\circ$ at XII pp.~272--274 are valid after correcting Cons~2 to say \emph{cocartesian}. Corollary~2 is valid with its stated conservativity and object-retract assumptions. No global initial object, cofibrancy or fibrancy of the terminal object, pushout-product axiom, or globally functorial factorization is required. The finite absolute diagrams used here have a least vertex: spans, squares, and their products. We do not assert the existence of arbitrary finite homotopy colimits in $\mathcal M$.
